Name: A farmer grew wheat to feed his OWN chickens and the Supreme Court ruled the government could still punish him for it
Copy:
Roscoe Filburn planted 12 acres more wheat than his federal quota allowed on his Ohio farm, and fed the extra to his own livestock instead of selling any of it

He argued that grain he never put on the market was not interstate commerce, so Congress had no business setting how much of it he could grow

The Supreme Court ruled against him unanimously in 1942, reasoning that if enough farmers did the same the effect on the national wheat market would be substantial
CTA:
Support farmers who feed their own land

Find them near you with Localize
context: Wickard v. Filburn, 317 U.S. 111 (1942). Ohio farmer Roscoe Filburn exceeded his Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938 wheat quota by 12 acres and used the surplus on his own farm. The Court ruled unanimously that Congress could regulate it under the Commerce Clause via the aggregation principle. Sources: Justia and FindLaw case texts, National Constitution Center, Institute for Justice. LEFT OUT: the penalty amount, which varies across accounts. Name: Eighteen starving farmers signed a secret pact in fingerprints, agreeing to prison or death, just so they could farm their own plots
Copy:
Xiaogang in Anhui province was so poor that families walked the countryside begging after each harvest, and 67 villagers had died of hunger during the Great Leap Forward

On 24 November 1978 the heads of eighteen households secretly agreed to split the commune's land into family plots, hand over a quota, and keep whatever they grew past it

They wrote that if it cost them death or prison the others would raise their children to eighteen, and the next harvest beat the previous five years put together
CTA:
Support families farming their own ground

You can see them near you with Localize
context: Xiaogang village, Anhui, China. On 24 November 1978 eighteen household heads signed a secret pledge, sealed with fingerprints, dividing commune land into family plots; it included a promise to raise each other's children to 18 if the signatories were imprisoned or executed. The village had lost 67 people to hunger in the Great Leap Forward. The following harvest exceeded the previous five combined. Sources: NPR Planet Money, China.org.cn, Marginal Revolution. Name: Private garden plots were 3 percent of Soviet farmland and they produced two thirds of the country's eggs
Copy:
Soviet households were allowed small subsidiary plots alongside the collective farms, and in 1966 those plots covered a little over 3 percent of all sown land in the country

From that sliver they produced 40 percent of the meat, 39 percent of the milk and 66 percent of the eggs the USSR grew that year

By the end of the Soviet period household plots still accounted for roughly a quarter of the country's entire agricultural output
CTA:
Support small growers working small ground

Find the ones near you on Localize
context: 1966 figures: the Soviet private sector produced 40% of the USSR's meat, 39% of its milk and 66% of its eggs on slightly more than 3% of total sown land. Personal subsidiary farming accounted for about 26% of agricultural output at the end of the Soviet period. Sources: Slavic Review, 'The Private Sector in Soviet Agriculture'; Soviet Studies via JSTOR; Oxford Academic, 'Russia's Unknown Agriculture'. LEFT OUT: widely quoted 1959 figures traced only to a partisan source. DEDUPE: checked khrushchev, private plot. No hits.

Name: In 1649 a group of Englishmen started planting vegetables on common land, and the landowners drove them off it
Copy:
On 1 April 1649 about thirty or forty people led by Gerrard Winstanley began digging the common land on St George's Hill in Surrey and planting carrots, beans and parsnips

Food prices had reached record highs, and they argued that with the king executed the land ought to feed the poorest people rather than sit idle

Local landowners and the new Commonwealth government moved against them, and after losing in court they gave up the hill that August
CTA:
Support growers working land that feeds people

See the ones near you on Localize
context: The Diggers. On 1 April 1649 roughly 30 to 40 people led by Gerrard Winstanley cultivated common land at St George's Hill, Walton-on-Thames, Surrey, planting carrots, beans and parsnips during a period of record food prices. Landowners and the Commonwealth government opposed them; after losing in court they left the hill in August 1649 and were later dispersed from Cobham by force and legal harassment. Sources: Britannica, Elmbridge Museum, Aeon. DEDUPE: checked winstanley, digger. No hits.

Name: The Dutch offered farmers up to 120 percent of what their farm was worth, on the condition they never farm anywhere in Europe again
Copy:
After a 2019 court ruling found the Netherlands was breaking EU law on nitrogen, the government set aside about 25 billion euros to cut emissions from livestock farming

Its buyout pays 100 to 120 percent of a livestock business's value and lets the farmer keep the land, provided emissions there fall by as much as 85 percent

Anyone who takes the money agrees not to run that business again in the Netherlands or anywhere else in the European Union
CTA:
Support livestock farmers staying on their land

See them in your area on Localize
context: The Dutch nitrogen buyout. A 2019 ruling by the highest Dutch administrative court found the government was breaching EU law on nitrogen deposition. The state earmarked about 25 billion euros; the voluntary buyout pays 100 to 120 percent of business value, the farmer keeps the land subject to emission cuts of up to 85 percent, and may not resume the business in the Netherlands or elsewhere in the EU. About 750 farms had signed up by end of 2023. Sources: Euronews, European Commission, USDA FAS. DEDUPE: checked nitrogen. Hits were fertilizer chemistry, unrelated.

Name: Mexico banned modified corn from its tortillas and a trade panel ruled it had no right to
Copy:
A February 2023 presidential decree barred genetically engineered corn from dough and tortillas in Mexico and told agencies to phase it out of other food uses and animal feed

The United States challenged the decree under its trade agreement with Mexico and Canada, and the panel issued its final report in December 2024

The panel sided with the United States on all seven claims, finding the measures were not based on science, and Mexico had 45 days to comply

A USMCA dispute panel issued its final report on 20 December 2024, agreeing with the United States on all seven claims and finding the measures were not science-based; Mexico had 45 days to comply. Sources: USDA press release of 20 December 2024, Wilson Center, National Agricultural Law Center, Cambridge AJIL. DEDUPE: checked usmca. No hits.

Name: Ghana's farmers blocked a seed law for five years, then it passed anyway under a different name
Copy:
A Plant Breeders Bill granting breeders exclusive rights over the varieties they register was withdrawn in 2015 after farmer unions and civil society groups fought it

It returned in 2019 as the Plant Variety Protection Bill, and parliament passed it on 2 November 2020 over the same objections

Ghana then joined the international plant variety treaty behind the law in December 2021, binding the country to its rules on who may sell protected seed
CTA:
Support farmers who keep their own seed

Find who is near you on Localize
context: Ghana's Plant Breeders Bill was withdrawn in 2015 after opposition from the Food Sovereignty Platform, including GAWU and the Peasant Farmers Association of Ghana. It was reintroduced in 2019 as the Plant Variety Protection Bill and passed on 2 November 2020. Ghana deposited its instrument of accession to the UPOV Convention on 3 November 2021, acceding on 3 December 2021. Sources: APBREBES, Geoforum (ScienceDirect, peer-reviewed), Peasant Farmers Association statement. DEDUPE: checked plant breeder. No hits.

Name: An American crayfish is wiping out Britain's native one, and it is illegal to trap them without a licence
Copy:
Signal crayfish escaped into British waters in the 1970s, outcompete the native white-clawed crayfish for food and habitat, and carry a plague that is fatal to them

Trapping them without a licence from the Environment Agency is an offence, and people have been prosecuted and fined for doing it

Commercial trapping for food is not permitted either, partly because moving the animals spreads the plague and taking the big ones lets the small ones multiply
CTA:
Support fishermen and shellfish harvesters

Your local ones are on Localize
context: Non-native American signal crayfish escaped into UK waters in the 1970s and have driven a decline in native white-clawed crayfish, which they outcompete and infect with crayfish plague. Environment Agency licences are required to trap them; unlicensed trapping is prosecuted. Commercial trapping for human consumption is not permitted, because moving the animals spreads plague and removing larger crayfish, which predate the smaller ones, can increase the population. Sources: gov.uk Environment Agency prosecution notices, Angling Trust guidance. DEDUPE: checked crayfish. No hits.

Name: Farm workers occupied a duke's unplanted estate until the village got the land, and their jobless rate fell to a fraction of Spain's
Copy:
From the 1970s labourers in Marinaleda in southern Spain occupied land held by absentee owners, including a large estate of the Duke of Infantado that sat mostly unplanted

The land ended up with the village and is worked by the El Humoso cooperative, which deliberately picks labour-heavy crops so the work stretches to more people

In 2012, with Spain at about 25 percent unemployment and Andalusia at 34, Marinaleda was running near 5 percent
CTA:
Support cooperative farms and the people on them

Find them on Localize
context: Marinaleda, Seville province, Andalusia. Farm labourers organised by Juan Manuel Sanchez Gordillo occupied absentee-owned land from the 1970s, including part of the Duke of Infantado's estate, which was eventually transferred to the town and is farmed by the El Humoso cooperative, which chooses labour-intensive crops to maximise jobs. In August 2012 local unemployment was about 5 percent against roughly 25 percent nationally and 34 percent in Andalusia. Sources: openDemocracy, Public Books, Andalucia.com. Name: A province chief let farming families keep what they grew, was forced to denounce himself for it, and got his medals 30 years after he died
Copy:
Kim Ngoc led the Communist Party in Vietnam's Vinh Phuc province from 1959 and handed collective land out to individual households to farm under contract

Output rose, but the national leadership condemned the scheme as a breach of the law and he was made to criticise his own wrong political line

He died in 1979, was rehabilitated in 1995 with the Order of Independence, and was awarded the Order of Ho Chi Minh in 2009
CTA:

context: Kim Ngoc (1917-1979) was Communist Party secretary of Vinh Phuc province, Vietnam, from 1959 to 1977, and introduced household contracting (khoan ho). The policy was halted, Le Duan condemned it as lawbreaking, and Kim Ngoc had to self-criticise. He was rehabilitated in 1995 and decorated posthumously with the Order of Independence (1995) and the Order of Ho Chi Minh (2009).
